[1] The bus left town at four in the morning, when the streets were still empty and deserted and the only light came from a bakery whose ovens had been lit an hour before. Most of the passengers slept. I could not, I had waited two years to see the salt flat, and I did not intend to miss the moment the sky first showed it to me.

[2] The flat is the bed of a lake that dried up thousands of years ago, leaving behind a crust of salt that stretches more than a hundred kilometers in every direction. In the dry season it is a plain of white hexagons, each edged by a low ridge where the crust buckled as it dried. In the wet season the rains leaves a few centimeters of water on top of the crust, and the whole surface becomes a mirror. [A] Visitors who arrive in the wet season are often unsettled by the horizon, which disappears entirely on a still morning.

[3] We arrived as the first gray light was spreading. The driver stopped the bus a kilometer out onto the flat and told us to walk. I stepped down and felt the crust crunch beneath my boots; it was firmer than I had expected, more like packed gravel than snow. Ahead of me the other passengers had spread out. Each becoming a small dark figure standing on its own reflection. [B]

[4] Then the sun came up. For perhaps ten minutes the sky and the ground were the same shade of orange, and there was no way to tell where one ended and the other began. A woman near me totally lost it. A man knelt down and photographed his own shoes. Nobody spoke to anyone else; we were each too busy looking. [C]

[5] By eight o'clock the light had hardened and the mirror had become an ordinary, if very large, puddle. The driver honked twice. On the way back to town the bakery was open, and we bought bread that was still warm while the flat behind us shrank to a white line and then to nothing. [D]

I had seen the videos: soggy boats folding in half, laughing teenagers sinking in three feet of water. It looked like chaos. Then, because I had objected the loudest, I was put in charge of it.

[2] The rules we wrote were simple. Each team could use only corrugated cardboard, duct tape, and paint, the boat had to carry two people the length of the pool, and anything that sank had to be fished out by its own crew. We set the date for the last Friday in May, and I spent April worrying about getting permits, hiring lifeguards, and trash bags.

[3] Sign-ups were slow at first. By the end of the second week, however, we had twenty-three teams, including one made up of four teachers whom insisted on being called the Faculty Fleet. The art room became a shipyard. Every afternoon I walked through it and saw boats taking shape: a Viking longship with a cardboard dragon's head, a pink submarine that its builders hoped would float, and a plain brown box that its builders called the Minimalist.

[4] On the night of the race the bleachers were full, and the pool deck smelled of chlorine and wet paint. The longship went first and made it to the far wall like a total boss before its dragon's head fell off. The submarine sank immediately, exactly as everyone except its builders had predicted. [A] The Faculty Fleet capsized at the halfway mark, and the crowd cheered louder for the teachers' swim to the ladder than for any finish. [B] Then the Minimalist, paddled by two quiet sophomores, crossed the pool in forty seconds without taking on a drop of water.

[5] I had expected chaos, and I got it. What I had not expected was how much I would enjoy it. [C] Cleaning up afterward, with the wreckage of twenty-three boats piled by the fence, I was relieved that it was over. [D]

passage_title: How a Swarm Chooses a Home
passage:
[1] In late spring a crowded honeybee colony splits in two. The old queen leaves the hive with roughly half of the workers, and the group settles in a dense, humming cluster on a nearby branch. The swarm now faces an urgent problem: it has no home, no stored food, and only a few days' time remaining before its energy runs out. Honey, of course, is what most people think of when they picture a hive. Within a few kilometers it must find a good cavity, and it must agree on one.

[2] The search falls to a few hundred scouts, the oldest and most experienced foragers in the swarm. Each scout that discovers a hollow tree or a gap in a wall looks at it carefully, walking its interior and estimating its volume by the length of her walks. If the cavity is promising, she returns to the cluster and performs a waggle dance. The dance—a series of figure-eight runs on the surface of the cluster—encodes the direction and distance of the site. Scouts that return from the best sites, dance the longest.

[3] Bees are fascinating creatures in many ways. A long dance draws more idle scouts to fly out and judge the site for themselves; a short dance draws fewer scouts. Crucially, no scout takes another's word: each recruit makes her own visit and dances with an enthusiasm that reflects her own judgment. A scout who has visited a poor site dances briefly and then stops. Which means that a mediocre site gradually loses its advertisers while a superior one gains them.

[4] The swarm does not wait for every scout to agree. Once fifteen or twenty scouts have gathered at the same site, they return and produce a high-pitched piping signal that tells the thousands of waiting bees to warm their flight muscles. Within an hour the whole cluster lifts off at once, and the scouts streak back and forth through the cloud, steering ten thousand bees toward a hole in a tree that almost none of them have ever seen.

[5] What is remarkable is that no single bee ever compares the sites. The queen plays no part in the choice. The decision emerges from hundreds of independent inspections, each one weighted by the honest length of a dance, and it is usually the best available site that wins.

choices: a few days' worth of time before
a few days, which is not long, before
explanation: "A few days" already names a length of time, so "time remaining," "worth of time," and "which is not long" repeat what the phrase says. "Before its energy runs out" then supplies the deadline. The plain "a few days before" is complete and free of repetition.

[1] In late spring a crowded honeybee colony splits in two. The old queen leaves the hive with roughly half of the workers, and the group settles in a dense, humming cluster on a nearby branch. The swarm now faces an urgent problem: it has no home, no stored food, and only a few days' time remaining before its energy runs out. Honey, of course, is what most people think of when they picture a hive. Within a few kilometers it must find a good cavity, and it must agree on one.

[2] The search falls to a few hundred scouts, the oldest and most experienced foragers in the swarm. Each scout that discovers a hollow tree or a gap in a wall looks at it carefully, walking its interior and estimating its volume by the length of her walks. If the cavity is promising, she returns to the cluster and performs a waggle dance. The dance—a series of figure-eight runs on the surface of the cluster—encodes the direction and distance of the site. Scouts that return from the best sites, dance the longest.

[3] Bees are fascinating creatures in many ways. A long dance draws more idle scouts to fly out and judge the site for themselves; a short dance draws fewer scouts. Crucially, no scout takes another's word: each recruit makes her own visit and dances with an enthusiasm that reflects her own judgment. A scout who has visited a poor site dances briefly and then stops. Which means that a mediocre site gradually loses its advertisers while a superior one gains them.
